explanation.overview: The tissue-selective effects of tamoxifen (SERM) mean it is anti-estrogenic in breast but pro-estrogenic in bone, endometrium, and lipid metabolism. Raloxifene has less endometrial agonist activity.
explanation.highYield: Tamoxifen = SERM → agonist on endometrium → endometrial hyperplasia/cancer risk. Annual gynecologic monitoring recommended.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Any abnormal uterine bleeding in a patient on tamoxifen requires prompt evaluation, including endometrial biopsy.

questions.question: Fulvestrant is an estrogen receptor antagonist used in metastatic breast cancer. Its unique mechanism is:

options.text: Binding to ER and promoting its degradation, leading to complete receptor downregulation
options.explanation: Fulvestrant is a selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) that binds to the estrogen receptor, inhibiting its dimerization and nuclear translocation, and accelerating its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.

options.text: Competitive antagonism of ER without degradation
options.explanation: Tamoxifen does this; fulvestrant causes degradation.
Aromatase inhibitors work by blocking estrogen synthesis.
GnRH agonists suppress ovaries; fulvestrant acts on the receptor.
Fulvestrant is an anti-estrogen, not anti-androgen.

explanation.overview: Fulvestrant is used in postmenopausal women with HR+ advanced breast cancer after progression on endocrine therapy. It is administered intramuscularly monthly.
explanation.highYield: Fulvestrant = SERD → ER degradation (no agonist activity). Used after AI resistance. IM injection.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Fulvestrant can cause injection site reactions. It is combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors for enhanced efficacy.

questions.question: Lenalidomide and pomalidomide are immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs) used in multiple myeloma. Their multiple effects include:

options.text: Cereblon-mediated degradation of Ikaros/Aiolos, anti-angiogenesis, and immune stimulation
options.explanation: IMiDs bind to cereblon (CRBN), a component of the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, altering its substrate specificity to degrade transcription factors Ikaros and Aiolos. They also inhibit angiogenesis and enhance T-cell and NK-cell activity.
Proteasome inhibition is the mechanism of bortezomib.
Alkylation is the mechanism of cyclophosphamide.
Microtubule stabilization is the action of taxanes.
CD20 targeting is the action of rituximab.

explanation.overview: Thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide are IMiDs with activity in multiple myeloma and del(5q) MDS. Lenalidomide is more potent and less neurotoxic than thalidomide. Pomalidomide is used in relapsed/refractory disease.
explanation.highYield: IMiDs (lenalidomide) → CRBN-Ikaros/Aiolos degradation, anti-angiogenesis, immune stimulation. Toxicities: myelosuppression, thrombosis, teratogenicity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: DVT prophylaxis (aspirin or anticoagulation) is recommended with lenalidomide in combination with steroids. All IMiDs are pregnancy category X.

questions.question: Venetoclax is a BCL-2 inhibitor used in CLL and AML. Its mechanism is:

options.text: Selectively binding BCL-2, displacing pro-apoptotic proteins, leading to apoptosis
options.explanation: Venetoclax is a BH3-mimetic that binds to the hydrophobic groove of BCL-2, releasing BIM and other pro-apoptotic proteins, which then activate BAX/BAK to permeabilize the mitochondrial membrane and trigger apoptosis.
BTK inhibition is the mechanism of ibrutinib.
PI3Kδ inhibition is the mechanism of idelalisib.
CD20 targeting is the action of rituximab.
Proteasome inhibition is the mechanism of bortezomib.

explanation.overview: Venetoclax is highly effective in CLL with 17p deletion and in combination with hypomethylating agents or low-dose cytarabine in elderly AML. It causes rapid tumor lysis syndrome (TLS).
explanation.highYield: Venetoclax = BCL-2 inhibitor → apoptosis of CLL/AML cells. Major risk: tumor lysis syndrome. Dose ramp-up required.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: TLS prophylaxis (hydration, allopurinol/rasburicase) and monitoring are mandatory during venetoclax initiation and dose escalation.

questions.question: Ibrutinib is a Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor used in B-cell malignancies. Its common adverse effects include:

options.explanation: Ibrutinib irreversibly inhibits BTK, which is also involved in platelet aggregation (via GPVI) and cardiac function. Atrial fibrillation, bleeding, and infections are common.
Cardiomyopathy is not a primary feature; atrial fibrillation is.
Renal toxicity is not typical.
Neuropathy is not a major side effect.
Pulmonary toxicity is rare.

explanation.overview: Ibrutinib is a first-generation BTK inhibitor used in CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Second-generation BTK inhibitors (acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) have improved selectivity and fewer off-target effects.
explanation.highYield: Ibrutinib = BTK inhibitor → blocks B-cell receptor signaling. Toxicities: atrial fibrillation, bleeding (inhibits platelet aggregation), diarrhea, infections.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Avoid concurrent use of anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents if possible. Hold ibrutinib before surgery. Acalabrutinib has less atrial fibrillation.

questions.question: Ruxolitinib is a JAK1/2 inhibitor used in myelofibrosis and polycythemia vera. Its mechanism is:

options.text: Inhibiting JAK-STAT signaling, reducing splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms
options.explanation: Ruxolitinib inhibits Janus kinases (JAK1 and JAK2), which are constitutively activated in myeloproliferative neoplasms, leading to reduced cytokine signaling and decreased splenomegaly and symptoms.
BCR-ABL is the target of imatinib.
FLT3 inhibitors (midostaurin) are used in AML.
VEGF blockade is the mechanism of bevacizumab.
CDK4/6 inhibitors are used in breast cancer.

explanation.overview: Ruxolitinib is approved for intermediate/high-risk myelofibrosis and for polycythemia vera after hydroxyurea failure. It improves quality of life and reduces spleen size.
explanation.highYield: Ruxolitinib = JAK1/2 inhibitor → blocks JAK-STAT signaling. Used in myelofibrosis, PV. Cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia) are dose-limiting.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ruxolitinib can cause immunosuppression and reactivation of infections (tuberculosis, hepatitis B). Dose adjustment is required for renal/hepatic impairment.

questions.question: Trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) is an antibody-drug conjugate. It delivers the cytotoxic agent DM1 (a maytansinoid) to HER2-positive cells. The advantage is:

options.text: Targeted delivery of a potent antimicrotubule agent, reducing systemic toxicity
options.explanation: T-DM1 links trastuzumab to DM1, a microtubule inhibitor. The antibody delivers the toxin specifically to HER2-overexpressing cells, allowing effective killing with less systemic toxicity than free DM1.
T-DM1 is given intravenously.

options.text: It does not require HER2 positivity
options.explanation: It specifically targets HER2-positive cells.
Cardiotoxicity can still occur.

options.text: It is an immune checkpoint inhibitor
options.explanation: It is a conjugated antibody, not a checkpoint inhibitor.

explanation.overview: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) combine the specificity of a monoclonal antibody with the potency of a cytotoxic drug. T-DM1 is standard second-line therapy for HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer.
explanation.highYield: T-DM1 = trastuzumab + DM1 (anti-microtubule) → targeted intracellular delivery. Toxicities: thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, neuropathy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: T-DM1 can cause peripheral neuropathy and interstitial lung disease. It is contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers due to DM1 metabolism.

questions.question: Filgrastim (G-CSF) is used in chemotherapy to:

options.text: Stimulate neutrophil production and reduce the duration of neutropenia
options.explanation: Filgrastim is a recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor that promotes proliferation and differentiation of myeloid progenitor cells, accelerating neutrophil recovery after myelosuppressive chemotherapy.
Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim) and IL-11 (oprelvekin) increase platelets.
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) increase red blood cells.
It specifically targets neutropenia, not all side effects.
G-CSF does not directly kill tumor cells; it supports neutrophil recovery.

explanation.overview: G-CSF is used as primary prophylaxis (when febrile neutropenia risk >20%) or secondary prophylaxis after neutropenic events. Pegfilgrastim is a longer-acting form requiring a single dose per cycle.
explanation.highYield: Filgrastim (G-CSF) → stimulates neutrophil recovery. Given 24-72 hours after chemotherapy. Pegfilgrastim is long-acting.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bone pain is a common side effect. Avoid G-CSF within 24 hours of chemotherapy (scheduling varies) to prevent myeloid progenitor sensitization.

questions.question: Dexrazoxane is used as a cardioprotectant in patients receiving anthracyclines. Its mechanism is:

options.text: Iron chelation, reducing free radical formation
options.explanation: Dexrazoxane is an EDTA analog that chelates iron, preventing the formation of anthracycline-iron complexes that generate reactive oxygen species, thereby reducing cardiac toxicity.
It works by chelation, not direct scavenging.
While it is a topoisomerase II catalytic inhibitor, its cardioprotection is from iron chelation.
It does not alter doxorubicin metabolism.
Not the mechanism.

explanation.overview: Dexrazoxane is given prior to anthracycline administration in patients who have received a high cumulative dose or have cardiac risk factors. It also has a role in treating anthracycline extravasation.
explanation.highYield: Dexrazoxane = iron chelator → prevents anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity. Also used for extravasation treatment.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dexrazoxane can cause myelosuppression and may slightly reduce anthracycline efficacy in some settings. It is recommended when cumulative doxorubicin exceeds 300 mg/m².

questions.question: Which of the following agents is classified as a 'differentiating agent' and is used in acute promyelocytic leukemia?

options.explanation: ATRA induces differentiation of leukemic promyelocytes by targeting the PML-RARα fusion protein, leading to degradation of the oncoprotein and maturation of the malignant cells.
Arsenic trioxide also degrades PML-RARα but is considered an apoptosis-inducing agent, not solely a differentiating agent.
Imatinib is a TKI for CML.
Decitabine is a hypomethylating agent.
Vorinostat is an HDAC inhibitor.

explanation.overview: ATRA is the prototype differentiation therapy. Combined with arsenic trioxide, it achieves cure rates >90% in low/intermediate-risk APL without conventional chemotherapy.
explanation.highYield: ATRA = differentiation therapy for APL (t(15;17) PML-RARα). Can cause differentiation syndrome (fever, respiratory distress, effusions) → treat with dexamethasone.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Differentiation syndrome (formerly retinoic acid syndrome) is a potentially fatal complication occurring 1-2 weeks after starting ATRA. Early recognition and high-dose dexamethasone are critical.

questions.question: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL used in cancer-related bone disease. Its primary indication is:

options.text: Prevention of skeletal-related events in bone metastases and giant cell tumor of bone
options.explanation: Denosumab inhibits RANKL, preventing osteoclast activation and bone resorption. It reduces fractures, spinal cord compression, and need for radiation in solid tumors with bone metastases.
It can be used but bisphosphonates are often first-line for acute hypercalcemia.

options.text: Induction of bone formation in osteoporosis
options.explanation: Denosumab is an antiresorptive, not an anabolic agent.
Not an indication.

options.text: Treatment of multiple myeloma bone lesions
options.explanation: Denosumab is used in solid tumors; zoledronic acid is more established in myeloma.

explanation.overview: Denosumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds RANKL, inhibiting osteoclastogenesis. It is administered subcutaneously every 4 weeks and does not require renal monitoring like bisphosphonates.
explanation.highYield: Denosumab = anti-RANKL → inhibits bone resorption. Used for bone metastases, GCTB. Risk of hypocalcemia, osteonecrosis of jaw (ONJ).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation is mandatory to prevent hypocalcemia. Dental evaluation before initiation reduces ONJ risk.

questions.question: Pralatrexate is a novel antifolate approved for peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Its advantage over methotrexate is:

options.text: Improved cellular uptake via reduced folate carrier (RFC) and retained in tumor cells longer
options.explanation: Pralatrexate was designed to have higher affinity for RFC and enhanced polyglutamation, leading to more selective accumulation and retention in cancer cells compared to methotrexate.

options.text: It does not require leucovorin rescue
options.explanation: Leucovorin is used to manage toxicity.

options.text: It is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor
options.explanation: It is an antifolate, not a TKI.
Myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia, is dose-limiting.
It is a small molecule.

explanation.overview: Pralatrexate is the first drug approved specifically for relapsed/refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma. It is structurally similar to methotrexate but with enhanced membrane transport and intracellular accumulation.
explanation.highYield: Pralatrexate = antifolate with high RFC affinity → better tumor cell uptake. Mucositis, thrombocytopenia are dose-limiting. Supplement with folate and B12.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients must receive folic acid and vitamin B12 supplementation to reduce toxicity. Severe mucositis is common and can be dose-limiting.

questions.question: A patient receiving pembrolizumab develops severe fatigue, hypotension, and hyponatremia. Adrenal insufficiency is suspected. The most likely immune-related etiology is:

options.text: Hypophysitis leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency
options.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors can cause hypophysitis, most commonly with ipilimumab, but also with PD-1 inhibitors. It presents with fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia, and low ACTH/cortisol. Central hypothyroidism and hypogonadism may also occur.
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) is less common than hypophysitis as an irAE.
Must be ruled out, but hypophysitis is a known irAE.
Cardiomyopathy does not cause hyponatremia as the primary feature.
Diabetes insipidus would present with polyuria and hypernatremia.

explanation.overview: Immune-related hypophysitis results in deficiency of ACTH, TSH, LH/FSH. Diagnosis: low morning cortisol, low ACTH, low TSH with low free T4. MRI shows pituitary enlargement. Management: high-dose corticosteroids and hormone replacement.
explanation.highYield: Checkpoint inhibitor hypophysitis → secondary adrenal insufficiency (fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia). Check AM cortisol, ACTH. Treat with corticosteroids.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Adrenal crisis can be prevented by stress-dose steroids during illness. Thyroid function and gonadal axes should also be assessed.

questions.question: Which of the following anticancer agents is a monoclonal antibody that targets the CD30 antigen and delivers a microtubule inhibitor (monomethyl auristatin E) to lymphoma cells?

options.explanation: Brentuximab vedotin is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) that links an anti-CD30 antibody to MMAE, a potent antimicrotubule agent. It is used in Hodgkin lymphoma and anaplastic large cell lymphoma.
Rituximab is a naked anti-CD20 antibody.
T-DM1 targets HER2 with DM1.
Bevacizumab targets VEGF-A.
Cetuximab targets EGFR.

explanation.overview: Brentuximab vedotin delivers the cytotoxic payload MMAE to CD30-expressing cells. CD30 is highly expressed on Reed-Sternberg cells in Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.highYield: Brentuximab vedotin = anti-CD30 + MMAE (anti-microtubule ADC). Used in Hodgkin lymphoma, ALCL. Peripheral neuropathy is dose-limiting.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Progressive peripheral neuropathy can require dose modification. The drug is given intravenously every 3 weeks.

questions.question: Inotuzumab ozogamicin is an ADC that targets CD22 and delivers calicheamicin. It is used in:

options.explanation: Inotuzumab ozogamicin binds CD22 on B-ALL cells, internalizes, and releases calicheamicin, which causes double-strand DNA breaks. It is approved for relapsed/refractory B-ALL.
CML is treated with TKIs.
APL is treated with ATRA and arsenic.
MDS is treated with hypomethylating agents, not anti-CD22.
Myeloma therapies include proteasome inhibitors, IMiDs.

explanation.overview: Inotuzumab ozogamicin is a CD22-directed ADC linked to calicheamicin, a potent DNA-damaging agent. It is used in relapsed/refractory B-ALL, with high response rates.
explanation.highYield: Inotuzumab ozogamicin = anti-CD22 + calicheamicin (DNA breaks). Used in B-ALL. Major toxicity: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (VOD), especially if followed by HSCT.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Veno-occlusive disease (VOD) of the liver is a serious risk; avoidance of dual hepatotoxic agents and careful bridging to transplant are necessary.

questions.question: Radium-223 is a radiopharmaceutical used in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases. It acts by:

options.text: Targeting areas of increased bone turnover and emitting alpha particles, causing localized DNA damage
options.explanation: Radium-223 is a calcium mimetic that preferentially incorporates into bone metastases where there is active bone remodeling. It emits high-energy alpha particles with a short range, sparing surrounding normal tissue.

options.text: Emitting beta particles that destroy tumor cells
options.explanation: Radium-223 is an alpha emitter; beta emitters include samarium-153.
Hormonal therapy is separate.
Denosumab blocks RANKL.
It does not stimulate bone formation.

explanation.overview: Radium-223 is the first alpha-emitting radionuclide approved for cancer therapy. It improves overall survival and delays skeletal events in mCRPC patients with symptomatic bone metastases and no visceral metastases.
explanation.highYield: Radium-223 = alpha emitter → targets bone metastases → DNA damage. Improves survival in CRPC with bone mets. Myelosuppression is main toxicity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: It is not combined with abiraterone plus prednisone due to increased fracture risk. Monitor blood counts due to myelosuppression.

questions.question: Which chemotherapy agent is known for causing 'hand-foot syndrome' (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia) when given as a continuous infusion?

options.explanation: Hand-foot syndrome is a characteristic toxicity of continuous infusion 5-FU and capecitabine. It is less common with bolus 5-FU.
Methotrexate is not typically associated with hand-foot syndrome.
Cisplatin causes neuropathy and nephrotoxicity.
Doxorubicin causes cardiotoxicity and myelosuppression.
Vincristine causes neuropathy.

explanation.overview: Hand-foot syndrome presents with erythema, swelling, and desquamation of palms and soles. It is also a hallmark of capecitabine and pegylated liposomal doxorubicin.
explanation.highYield: Continuous 5-FU / capecitabine → hand-foot syndrome. Manage with dose interruption, emollients, cold compresses.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: For capecitabine, dose reduction and topical urea-based creams are used. In severe cases, chemotherapy may need to be stopped.

questions.question: Lomustine and carmustine are nitrosoureas that can cross the blood-brain barrier. Their dose-limiting toxicity is:

options.explanation: Nitrosoureas cause profound, prolonged, and cumulative myelosuppression, with nadirs occurring 4-6 weeks after administration.
Cardiotoxicity is not typical.
Carmustine can cause pulmonary fibrosis, but myelosuppression is dose-limiting.
Nephrotoxicity is not the main toxicity.
Neuropathy is not characteristic.

explanation.overview: Nitrosoureas are lipid-soluble alkylating agents used in brain tumors and lymphoma. They are unique for their ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and their delayed myelosuppression.
explanation.highYield: Carmustine/lomustine = nitrosoureas (CNS penetration). Dose-limiting = delayed myelosuppression (4-6 weeks). Also cause pulmonary fibrosis, renal toxicity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Carmustine wafers (Gliadel) are implanted into the brain for local treatment of glioblastoma. Systemic nitrosoureas require prolonged intervals between cycles.

questions.question: Pegaspargase is a PEGylated form of asparaginase. The PEGylation primarily serves to:

options.explanation: PEGylation increases the molecular size, reducing renal clearance and shielding the enzyme from immune recognition, leading to longer duration of action and fewer hypersensitivity reactions.
Potency is similar, but duration is prolonged.
It is still given intravenously or intramuscularly.
Toxicity profile is similar; the benefit is in dosing interval and immunogenicity.
PEGylation does not significantly increase CNS penetration.

explanation.overview: Pegaspargase is preferred in pediatric ALL due to its prolonged half-life (allowing 2-4 week intervals) and reduced immunogenicity compared to native E. coli asparaginase. It is used when hypersensitivity to native asparaginase occurs.
explanation.highYield: Pegaspargase = PEGylated asparaginase → longer half-life, less immunogenic. Still causes pancreatitis, thrombosis, hepatotoxicity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Despite PEGylation, hypersensitivity reactions can still occur. Erwinia asparaginase is an alternative for patients with severe reactions to E. coli-derived products.

questions.question: Romidepsin is unique among HDAC inhibitors because it is a prodrug activated by:

options.text: Reduction of a disulfide bond within cells
options.explanation: Romidepsin is a bicyclic depsipeptide that is reduced intracellularly to release a zinc-binding thiol group that potently inhibits histone deacetylases.
It is activated by reduction, not oxidation.
Activation is intracellular via glutathione reduction.
Not the mechanism.
It inhibits deacetylases.

explanation.overview: Romidepsin is a unique HDAC inhibitor with a disulfide bond that acts as a prodrug. It is approved for cutaneous and peripheral T-cell lymphomas.
explanation.highYield: Romidepsin = prodrug reduced intracellularly to active zinc-binding thiol → HDAC inhibition. Side effects: nausea, QT prolongation, thrombocytopenia.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: ECG monitoring is recommended because romidepsin can cause significant QT prolongation. Electrolyte imbalances should be corrected before dosing.

questions.question: Sipuleucel-T is an autologous cellular immunotherapy used in prostate cancer. Its mechanism is:

options.text: Activating patient's dendritic cells against prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP)
options.explanation: Sipuleucel-T involves collecting patient's peripheral blood mononuclear cells, exposing them ex vivo to a fusion protein of PAP and GM-CSF, then reinfusing the activated antigen-presenting cells to stimulate a T-cell response against prostate cancer.

options.text: Direct lysis of prostate cancer cells
options.explanation: It is an immunotherapy, not a direct cytotoxic agent.
It does not block androgen receptors.
PD-1 inhibitors are checkpoint blockers.
CYP17 inhibition is the mechanism of abiraterone.

explanation.overview: Sipuleucel-T is the first therapeutic cancer vaccine approved by the FDA. It improves overall survival in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer without affecting PSA levels or disease progression time.
explanation.highYield: Sipuleucel-T = autologous dendritic cell vaccine against PAP. Prolongs survival in mCRPC. Adverse effects: infusion reactions, flu-like symptoms.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The treatment involves three infusions at 2-week intervals. It is not recommended for patients with rapidly progressive disease needing immediate cytoreduction.

questions.question: Trabectedin is a marine-derived alkaloid used in soft tissue sarcoma and ovarian cancer. It exerts its effect by:

options.text: Binding to DNA minor groove and disrupting transcription-coupled repair
options.explanation: Trabectedin binds to the DNA minor groove, specifically to guanine-rich sequences, bending DNA toward the major groove and blocking transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (TC-NER), leading to lethal DNA breaks.
It does not inhibit topoisomerase II.
It is a minor groove binder, not an intercalator.
It does not alkylate DNA.
Not a microtubule inhibitor.

explanation.overview: Trabectedin (ET-743) is particularly active in translocation-related sarcomas (myxoid liposarcoma) and in BRCA-mutated cancers. It is metabolized by CYP3A4.
explanation.highYield: Trabectedin = minor groove binder → blocks TC-NER. Active in soft tissue sarcoma, ovarian cancer. Hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression are toxicities.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pre-medication with dexamethasone reduces hepatotoxicity. Avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Rhabdomyolysis has been reported.

questions.question: Copanlisib is a PI3K inhibitor used in relapsed follicular lymphoma. Unlike idelalisib (selective PI3Kδ), copanlisib inhibits:

options.explanation: Copanlisib inhibits both PI3K-α and PI3K-δ, and is given intravenously. Idelalisib is an oral PI3Kδ inhibitor. Copanlisib has a different toxicity profile, including hyperglycemia and hypertension due to PI3K-α inhibition.
Copanlisib is a pan-PI3K inhibitor.
BTK is targeted by ibrutinib.
BCL-2 is targeted by venetoclax.
JAK2 is targeted by ruxolitinib.

explanation.overview: Copanlisib is a pan-class I PI3K inhibitor with predominant activity against PI3K-α and PI3K-δ. It is approved for relapsed follicular lymphoma in patients who have received at least two prior therapies.
explanation.highYield: Copanlisib = PI3K-α/δ inhibitor (IV). Hyperglycemia, hypertension, infections. Idelalisib = PI3Kδ (oral) → colitis, pneumonitis, infections.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Monitor blood glucose and blood pressure during copanlisib infusion. Prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is recommended.

questions.question: Gilteritinib is a FLT3 inhibitor used in relapsed/refractory AML with FLT3 mutations. Its advantage over midostaurin is:

options.text: More selective and potent FLT3 inhibition, including FLT3-ITD and TKD mutations
options.explanation: Gilteritinib is a highly selective FLT3/AXL inhibitor with activity against both internal tandem duplication (ITD) and tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) mutations. It is used as monotherapy in relapsed/refractory AML.
Both are small molecule TKIs.
Myelosuppression is common with both.
IDH inhibitors are ivosidenib, enasidenib.
Gilteritinib is oral.

explanation.overview: FLT3 mutations (ITD, TKD) are common in AML. Midostaurin is a first-generation multi-kinase inhibitor; gilteritinib is a next-generation selective FLT3 inhibitor with higher response rates in relapsed setting.
explanation.highYield: Gilteritinib = FLT3/AXL inhibitor for relapsed/refractory FLT3-mutated AML. Midostaurin = multi-targeted, used upfront. Differentiation syndrome can occur with gilteritinib.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gilteritinib can cause posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and prolonged QT interval. ECG and symptom monitoring are essential.

questions.question: Ivosidenib and enasidenib are IDH inhibitors used in AML. They target:

options.text: IDH1 and IDH2 mutations, respectively, reducing 2-hydroxyglutarate
options.explanation: Ivosidenib inhibits mutant IDH1, enasidenib inhibits mutant IDH2. These mutations produce the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which impairs hematopoietic differentiation. Inhibition restores normal differentiation.
FLT3 inhibitors are gilteritinib, midostaurin.
BCR-ABL is targeted by imatinib.
No direct RAS inhibitors are approved.
NPM1 is a prognostic marker, not a direct drug target.

explanation.overview: IDH mutations are found in 15-20% of AML patients. IDH inhibitors promote differentiation of leukemic blasts, similar to ATRA in APL. They can cause differentiation syndrome.
explanation.highYield: Ivosidenib (IDH1), Enasidenib (IDH2) → reduce 2-HG, induce differentiation. Used in relapsed/refractory AML. Risk of differentiation syndrome, QT prolongation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Differentiation syndrome (fever, pulmonary infiltrates, effusions) is managed with corticosteroids and dose interruption. These agents are oral and require liver function monitoring.

questions.question: Selinexor is a selective inhibitor of nuclear export (SINE) that targets XPO1. It is used in multiple myeloma and DLBCL. Its mechanism is:

options.text: Blocking export of tumor suppressor proteins and growth regulators from the nucleus
options.explanation: Selinexor covalently binds to exportin-1 (XPO1/CRM1), preventing the nuclear export of tumor suppressor proteins (p53, p21, IκB) and growth regulatory mRNAs, leading to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
Proteasome inhibition is the mechanism of bortezomib.
CDK4/6 inhibitors are palbociclib, etc.
DNA alkylation is the action of cyclophosphamide.
Immune checkpoint blockade is the action of PD-1/CTLA-4 inhibitors.

explanation.overview: Selinexor is the first approved XPO1 inhibitor. It is used in combination with dexamethasone for penta-refractory multiple myeloma and as monotherapy for relapsed/refractory DLBCL.
explanation.highYield: Selinexor = XPO1 inhibitor → nuclear retention of tumor suppressors → apoptosis. Toxicities: nausea, fatigue, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Aggressive antiemetic prophylaxis is required. Dose is 100 mg weekly. It can cause significant weight loss and anorexia.
